title: Injury Risk: Injured, Recovering and Chronic Cases
brief: Which players are injured now, coming back from injury, on minutes limits or load management, or have chronic same-spot lower-body problems? Tiers must separate chronic cases (price down) from one-off injuries (do not overreact), and note who can use one of our 4 IL slots.
summary: Price down players with repeated injuries to the same lower-body spot, mainly knees, or an ongoing illness. Their risk stays even after a healthy season. One-off injuries from last season should not scare you off, but expect lower value while a player ramps up on a minutes limit. Our 4 IL slots only take players tagged O or injured, so use them for cheap end-of-draft stashes, never for Q players.

paragraphs.text: Be careful with players who have had repeated injuries or surgeries to the same lower-body part, especially the knee. The same goes for anyone with an ongoing mystery illness. Hand, finger, shoulder and oblique injuries do not matter much. Concussions matter a little. So in the tiers below, a shoulder or thumb injury does not count as chronic, but a second calf strain or another knee surgery does.

Repeated surgeries and problems in the same spot make future missed games more likely. Draft these players below their per-game value. A good season does not remove the risk of a degenerative injury, so keep the discount even after a healthy year. At our auction, set your cap for a chronic case below what his per-game line is worth. Do not raise it because he stayed healthy last season.

Back-to-back counts matter mostly for injury-prone players. Before you bid on a chronic case, count his team's back-to-backs, and look hardest at the ones in weeks 19 to 21. Our season ends on 2027-03-28. A player who sits every back-to-back loses games in exactly the weeks that decide our league.

sections.heading: One-off injuries and players coming back

paragraphs.text: The season is 25 weeks long. A player who starts it with a short-term injury should not fall too far on your board. One expert also says drafters are too scared of players coming back from injuries that cost them last season. You can be more confident than their ADPs suggest.

Injuries have a hidden cost. A player coming back usually has a minutes limit and misses back-to-backs while he ramps up. All of his numbers drop in that stretch, not just his games played. For a returner, take a few weeks of reduced production out of your price.

The experts do not fully agree. One side says the market overreacts to last season's injuries, so returners are bargains at ADP. The other side says to avoid players who start the season injured, and warns that minutes limits and missed back-to-backs lower a returner's value. Here is a working rule for our room. Bid a little above market for a player back from a one-off injury who is cleared with no stated limit. Discount him when a minutes cap or back-to-back rest has been announced.

Yahoo removed IL+. A player tagged out (O) or injured can go on IL right away. Questionable, doubtful and probable players cannot. We only have 2 bench spots, so a Q-tagged player with no clear return eats a bench or starting spot. Before the draft, check each target's Yahoo tag, not just the news.

Do not spend real money on a long-term injured player, and do not stash him at the cost of a useful spot. Keep him only in an empty IL slot and drop him as soon as you need the room. At our auction, that makes an O-tagged player a 1 USD final pick at most. Check that his expected return comes well before 2027-03-28. If he only comes back after our season ends, he is worth nothing to us.

As a general rule, do not load up on several players you have injury worries about. Before every bid on a chronic case, a returner or a load-managed player, count how many big risks you already own. If you already carry a couple, pass and let another manager take the next one. Daily lineups and 4 IL slots soften missed games, but they do not replace a starter who keeps sitting.
